name: Chapter 6 - The IS-LM model - Comprehensive MCQ Bank

questions.text: The IS-LM model is associated historically with:

options.c: Hicks' 1937 formalisation/interpretation of Keynes' General Theory
options.d: Kuznets' national-accounting work only

questions.text: The key contribution captured by IS-LM is the joint analysis of:

options.b: exports and imports without financial markets
options.c: the labour market and only long-run growth
options.d: the goods market and the financial/money market

questions.text: The IS-LM model is primarily a model of:

options.b: only the medium run with flexible prices
options.d: the demographic transition

questions.text: The IS-LM equilibrium combines equilibrium on:

options.a: the Solow saving and depreciation curves only
options.c: the current and capital accounts only
options.d: the goods market (IS) and the money market (LM)

questions.text: In the very short run of IS-LM, the course assumes:

options.a: goods prices and wages fixed, firm productive equipment given, financial-asset prices/interest rates flexible
options.b: technology endogenous and prices rising with output
options.c: all prices and capital fully flexible
options.d: wages flexible but interest rates fixed by definition

questions.text: A macroeconomic equilibrium in IS-LM means:

options.a: equilibrium in the goods market regardless of finance
options.d: simultaneous equilibrium in the macro markets included in the model

questions.text: The IS curve contains all (Y,r) combinations for which:

options.a: the balance of payments is zero
options.b: the goods market is in short-run equilibrium
options.d: the money market is in equilibrium

questions.text: The IS curve slopes downward because:

options.a: a lower real interest rate lowers investment
options.b: a lower real interest rate raises investment and aggregate demand, increasing equilibrium output
options.d: higher output reduces consumption

questions.text: A reduction in r shifts the economy along a given IS curve rather than shifting IS because:

options.b: r is an exogenous determinant excluded from investment
options.c: r is an axis variable whose effect on goods-market equilibrium is already embodied in the curve
options.d: IS never responds to interest rates

questions.text: The IS curve is flatter when the goods-market response to interest rates is stronger. Which change tends to flatten IS?

options.b: a higher interest sensitivity of investment b2
options.d: a lower marginal propensity to consume

questions.text: A higher marginal propensity to consume c1 tends to make the IS curve:

options.d: flatter, because interest-induced demand changes have a larger multiplier effect

questions.text: A lower tax sensitivity t1 tends to make IS:

options.d: flatter

questions.text: A higher induced-investment coefficient b1 tends to make IS:

options.d: flatter

questions.text: Which change shifts the IS curve to the right?

options.a: an increase in autonomous taxes T0
options.c: an increase in government spending G
options.d: an increase in the risk premium σ

questions.text: Which autonomous-demand change shifts IS to the right?

options.a: an increase in autonomous consumption C0
options.d: a fall in C0

questions.text: Which risk-premium change shifts IS to the right?

options.a: a decrease in money supply only
options.b: a decrease in the risk premium σ
options.d: an increase in autonomous money demand only

questions.text: A rise in autonomous taxes T0 shifts IS:

options.d: nowhere because taxes do not affect consumption

questions.text: The real money-demand equation used to build LM is:

options.d: M^d/P = M^s/P

questions.text: The parameter l1 measures:

options.a: the income sensitivity of money demand
options.d: the reserve ratio

questions.text: The parameter l2 measures:

options.c: the interest-rate sensitivity of money demand
options.d: the depreciation rate

questions.text: The LM curve contains all (Y,i) combinations for which:

options.c: the money market is in equilibrium
options.d: the goods market is in equilibrium

questions.text: The traditional LM curve slopes upward because:

options.a: higher interest rates raise money demand
options.d: higher output raises money demand, requiring a higher interest rate to restore equilibrium for a fixed money supply

questions.text: From the algebraic LM relation, a higher l1 makes LM:

options.d: steeper

questions.text: A higher interest sensitivity of money demand l2 makes LM:

options.d: flatter

questions.text: An increase in money supply M^s shifts the traditional LM curve:

options.d: not at all

questions.text: A fall in autonomous money demand L0 shifts LM:

options.d: IS left

questions.text: With nominal money supply fixed, a lower price level P increases real money balances M^s/P and shifts LM:

options.d: not at all

questions.text: A traditional upward-sloping LM implicitly corresponds to a central bank that:

options.c: fixes both money supply and interest rate simultaneously for all shocks
options.d: fixes money supply and allows the interest rate to adjust

questions.text: A horizontal LM corresponds to a central bank that:

options.a: assumes money demand independent of output
options.b: targets an interest rate and adjusts money supply as needed to maintain it
options.d: targets a fixed quantity of money only

questions.text: If output rises and the central bank wants to keep its target interest rate unchanged, it should:

options.a: shift IS left by reducing investment directly
options.d: increase money supply to accommodate the higher money demand

questions.text: When a central bank changes its target interest rate in the horizontal-LM representation:

options.b: the money market ceases to exist
options.d: the LM curve becomes vertical automatically

questions.text: A modelling complication is that IS is naturally derived using:

options.b: a longer-term risk-adjusted real rate, while the money market determines a short-term nominal rate
options.d: the same nominal rate by construction without assumptions

questions.text: To place IS and LM in one diagram, the course assumes:

options.a: long and short relevant rates can be linked and expected inflation is constant/known
options.b: money demand depends on the real rate only
options.c: expected inflation is always zero and risk is infinite
options.d: the real rate is unrelated to the nominal rate

questions.text: Using i = r + π^e, a higher expected inflation with i fixed implies:

options.c: a leftward IS shift by identity
options.d: a higher real interest rate

questions.text: The IS-LM equilibrium is the unique pair (Y,r) that:

options.d: simultaneously satisfies the IS and LM relationships

questions.text: An expansive monetary policy is one that:

options.a: reduces money supply and raises rates
options.b: supports economic activity, typically by shifting LM down/right
options.d: shifts IS left through higher taxes

questions.text: A restrictive monetary policy tends to:

options.a: shift LM up/left, raise the interest rate and reduce output in the standard model
options.b: lower the interest rate and raise output
options.d: shift IS right

questions.text: Monetary policy affects primarily:

options.a: the LM curve, leaving the IS relation unchanged at the moment of the monetary action
options.d: the production function

questions.text: The effectiveness of monetary policy is greater when:

options.a: LM is flatter and IS is steeper
options.b: IS is vertical and LM horizontal
options.c: LM is steeper and IS is flatter
options.d: both curves are vertical

questions.text: Why does a flatter IS make monetary policy more powerful?

options.a: It prevents investment from responding to rates.
options.d: A given interest-rate movement produces a larger change in goods-market equilibrium output.

questions.text: An expansive fiscal policy is defined as:

options.c: an increase in the fiscal deficit through higher G and/or lower taxes
options.d: a fall in the fiscal deficit

questions.text: Fiscal policy shifts:

options.d: IS while leaving LM unchanged initially

questions.text: The crowding-out effect of fiscal expansion refers to:

options.a: imports replacing exports in a closed economy
options.b: higher interest rates reducing private investment and offsetting part of the direct demand stimulus
options.c: lower interest rates increasing private investment
options.d: higher taxes caused by inflation

questions.text: Fiscal expansion has a larger effect on output when:

options.a: IS is flatter and LM is steeper
options.c: IS is steeper and LM is flatter
options.d: money demand is infinitely income-sensitive

questions.text: A flatter LM reduces crowding out because:

options.a: interest rates rise less in response to the fiscal-induced increase in output and money demand
options.d: investment is independent of rates

questions.text: The size of the fiscal effect depends on both:

options.d: the initial goods-market multiplier and the subsequent crowding-out through interest rates

questions.text: A policy mix is:

options.a: the sum of exports and imports
options.b: a mix of wages and profits in GDI
options.c: a combination of CPI and GDP deflator
options.d: a coordinated combination of fiscal and monetary policies to pursue multiple objectives

questions.text: The Clinton-Greenspan policy mix combined:

options.a: restrictive fiscal policy with expansive monetary policy
options.c: expansive fiscal and restrictive monetary policy
options.d: two restrictive policies

questions.text: The objective of that policy mix was to:

options.a: reduce the fiscal deficit while maintaining economic activity
options.c: raise the fiscal deficit and reduce output
options.d: increase natural unemployment

questions.text: In IS-LM terms, the Clinton fiscal consolidation shifts IS:

options.d: left

questions.text: The accompanying monetary expansion shifts LM:

options.d: down/right

questions.text: Evidence presented from a 1 percentage-point Federal Funds rate increase shows:

options.b: retail and output both rise immediately
options.d: retail spending contracts relatively quickly and output also falls, though more slowly

questions.text: The empirical response to a rate increase supports the very-short-run fixed-price assumption because:

options.d: the aggregate price level changes only modestly over roughly the first year

questions.text: The same evidence also motivates moving beyond IS-LM at longer horizons because:

options.b: price-level changes become important in short- and medium-run analysis
options.d: interest rates stop existing

questions.text: Suppose the IS relation is Y = 1000 − 50r and LM is r = 0.01Y − 5. The equilibrium output is:
With the same equations, the equilibrium real interest rate is approximately:
If fiscal expansion shifts IS right while LM is very steep, compared with a flat LM the policy produces:

options.c: a larger output increase and smaller rate increase
options.d: a smaller increase in output and larger interest-rate crowding out

questions.text: If money demand becomes more interest-sensitive (higher l2), LM becomes flatter. This tends to make:

options.b: fiscal policy more effective and monetary policy less effective, other things equal
options.d: fiscal policy less effective and monetary policy more effective

questions.text: (Select the incorrect answer) In the IS-LM model:

options.a: their intersection gives simultaneous equilibrium in the two markets
options.b: IS slopes downward in the standard representation
options.c: the IS curve is the set of money-market equilibria and LM is the set of goods-market equilibria
options.d: LM slopes upward when money supply is fixed
